Michael Moritz on why he doesn't think he'd succeed in venture today.

"The venture business that I got into way back when is very different from the venture business today. I think it's become much more difficult. 

We had a variety of benefits back in the '80s and '90s that don't exist today.

One of them being imperfect information. Pre-internet, unless you were very close to things, you didn't know what was happening. Today, everybody's got access to more or less the same information.

Number two, there are just so many more entities of all stripes. Individuals, two or three people banding together in a small firm, and at the other end of it, huge mutual funds pouring money into it.

40 years ago, it was possible to form a real relationship, a close relationship, with the people that you were getting into business with. That doesn't exist today. There are just too many intermediaries in between.

I think a moderately intelligent 14, 16-year-old who had his or her wits about him would've been able to succeed in the venture business in the mid-'80s."

Ripple’s $RLUSD supply just ripped 40% in the last 30 days, so I wanted to see what may have caused it, and I found a few potential catalysts:

→ @Ripple uses RLUSD as the primary stablecoin in its payments business, giving it an existing customer base to build demand around.

→ Ripple says some Ripple Prime derivatives clients already hold balances in RLUSD. It’s also used as collateral, giving clients a reason to keep funds available beyond making payments.

→ Ripple Treasury’s customers handle roughly $13T in annual transactions. That isn’t RLUSD volume, but moving some of those payments into RLUSD could support further demand.

There’s also a potential European rollout and a planned lending initiative with @ClearpoolFin and @cicadacredit. Both could add demand, though they don’t explain the growth already on this chart.

IMO, Ripple’s existing customer base is the interesting part. These companies already use its services, which could make adopting RLUSD an easier next step.

The 40% growth also comes from a relatively small base. Now I want to see whether regular usage keeps up with the growing supply.

It's an increasingly common take that AI hacking means cybersecurity is doomed.

I disagree. I think cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring once people get their shit together. And anyone who continues to hold cryptocurrency (including me, ~90% of my net worth) is implicitly making that bet.

Here's why I am making that bet.

First, the oversimplified punchy one-line statement:

If AI can prove Navier-Stokes and FLT, then AI can prove the statement "this program is secure" as a mathematical theorem. Even if the program is very complicated.

Now, the nuance:

(See also: https://t.co/6YPWgVT7rO )

The word "secure" is hiding all kinds of skeletons in the closet in terms of what it actually means. What does it mean for Signal (the encrypted messenger) to be "secure"?

The most basic definition you might think of is: no one who doesn't hold the recipient's secret key can read the contents of the message.

But:

* Did you remember to include _other_ critical forms of security? Can the adversary forge messages? Can the attacker prevent messages from reaching the recipient? Can they cause your client to crash by sending malformed messages?
* Have you made sure that your model of the adversary includes attackers that interfere with the protocol actively and not just passively? And attackers that interfere by replaying messages to you or the recipient that either of you sent over the wire at any point earlier?
* What if the adversary hacked (or _is_) the Signal server?
* How did you learn which public key belongs to the recipient in the first place? What if that process was tampered with?
* What if your device gets hacked at some point in the past or future - is your message still safe then?
* What if your key leaks because of a bug in your operating system? Or because you got a bugged version of the Signal client? Or what if the database is corrupted?
* Or the libraries, interpreter or compiler of the programming language you wrote it in?
* What if your key leaks because tiny perturbations in perceptible signals generated by the hardware leak mathematical relationships that can extract the key a few hundredths of a bit at a time?
* Are you hiding the *size* of the payload? Does that matter?
* You're definitely not hiding the identity of the sender and the recipient, and the exact time each message was sent (think: not just time-of-day, but also time deltas between one message and the next). Is that not enough to deduce a lot of important facts about what relationships you have, and what *kinds* of conversations you are having?

So ... even definitions can be over a thousand lines of code, and need deep careful thought to figure them out.

Working on making definitions more human-readable is of extreme importance - it's perhaps the only "high-level language" that matters right now.

But even still, even despite all of the above, for security-critical components, the definition is a much smaller attack surface than the implementation. Verifying that the definition is adequate is a much more tractable task than scanning over the code directly - and can become even more tractable with better tooling.

Definitions are also _additive_: if two groups have two different definitions A and B, then, well, you can just prove that the program satisfies both A and B. Code is not additive in this way: if a program is A + B, a bug in A _or_ B can sink the whole thing. Definitions are additive. And if you can't satisfy A and B at the same time, you've isolated the most important philosophical issue for your project to spend its next few weeks grappling with.

Sometimes, definitions are not much smaller than the implementation - UI components might be one example. But for many of the most critical components - message-passing protocols, sandboxes, cryptography like SNARKs and FHE - the asymmetry is real.

Historically, a large class of failures with this approach have come from people only verifying a small portion of their code, that they self-declared to be the security-critical portion, and ignoring the rest - and it turns out that something in the rest of the code is security-critical too.

This was reasonable back when verification was difficult and scarce. The solution today: sorry, you have to verify over literally your entire program, including database, networking, any caching layers, everything. Modern AI can do it.

So it's not about "the good guys find all the vulnerabilities before the bad guys do" - that could maybe work too, after all a finite program only has a finite number of vulns, but it's riskier - it's specifically an asymmetric strategy of making code that is much more resilient in the first place.

This is the kind of direction that Ethereum is going in for the next few years. There is no future for blockchains - especially blockchains with scalability and privacy - without doing this. We need to make software actually secure. And we have already made a lot of progress.

The old GDP formula was population growth + productivity growth + debt growth. 

It ran for decades and it worked beautifully for the most part... populations grew, people got more productive, and debt was there to smooth the edges.

In recent years demographics have weakened, productivity has stalled, and debt has ended up carrying the whole bloody thing. This is the crux of The Everything Code and it's exactly why we're stuck in this cycle, printing to service what we owe.

But there's a way out. The economic singularity version of the formula is population growth + productivity growth + debt growth + AI + robots. 

Productivity becomes how much intelligence you can produce per unit of energy, and suddenly the first two engines are back on.

We've seen this play out before. In the 1950s a generation walked out of the war and made a load of babies, GDP boomed, and the debt just got smaller and smaller as a share of the economy until nobody thought about it anymore.

Same thing's about to happen again. Except this time we have robots.

I wrote the whole thing up today, from 1929 to now. Link below.

Market color post-fomc sep 17 - another one that was for subscribers, but decided to make this public because i wanted to share my insights wrt. crypto

- it seems we really got a bullish rate hike; i will provide no macro color nor pontificate on the ramifications of further hikes, all i can do is interpret the consequences of such a result

- fed seems aligned to getting inflation back to 2%. imo what just matters for the coming weeks / months is the market digesting that we are entering a high rate regime; 

- quite frankly it is a bullish rate hike because it gets the overhang of uncertainty out of the way which markets hate. 

- i continue believing equities are resetting from the bull market - hence they are in very rangebound, choppy conditions. no trend can be trusted, and it's take profits regime. zooming out, it is a great area to start placing bids for the next eventual bull cycle 

- crypto continues to be the hot ball of money and in a trending market on its own. words really cannot describe how ephemereal this is - crypto outperformance amidst equity bloodshed. it is a much needed sight and i continue to believe market participants are very much sidelined on this move. it probably goes higher, for longer.

- more words have to be said about this crypto move. the fact is, after Trump, DATs, the market was quite rekt and needed time to heal. And during this period, it is clear that crypto products have found product market fit - whether through equity perps, prediction markets, or defi yield. either way, these products (all of which mostly have no token) are being used; 

- i believe that investors are too pre-occupied with price following narrative because crypto has always been price led for all of its making - coins have had no intrinsic value, and so you really only had an explanation after the move happened - "oh, saylor bought"; "oh, xxx event happened" and no intrinsic upgrades ;

- however, this time we actually have narrative leading price. the narrative is simple - crypto products have genuine usage in the few verticals we've seen. as such, these verticals are re-rating respectively; while the rest of the sector stays relatively still

- this imo is a sign of evolution in the crypto markets themselves.  yes there will be broad based rallies where things go up 50% - 100% - this was the rally from the beaten down -> "fairly valued" i.e because crypto was really so beat down, this 50% bear market bottom bounce is quite in-line

- but beyond that, the rally from "fairly valued" -> "overvalued" is only concentrated in a handful of coins, all of which align with the narratives that have been shown to have proven themselves. 

- to put it into perspective, of the top 100 coins, only 10 coins are up more than 50% in the past month. while that might seem alot, iin the past it would have been at least 20. above 500m mc, only 4 coins have 100%+ returns. 

- I believe that i myself had the wrong take - after DATs and the bear market, I thought that the crypto market was really done for. That was a naive view that didn't consider the otherside - the better view that I saw once I started writing for DefiLlama, was that there was actually broad usage of many crypto products, albeit most of them not having tokens, but how can you look at the products and conclude "yea crypto is being used but tokens are shit" 

- On top of that, founders are constantly iterating, and more than before we have a new frontier of founders who are paving the way on what tokens should be regardless of whether or not clarity was given. There is a general business sense if you're a good founder about the direction you should go now if you hold a token, and that continues to improve the token landscape. 

- Now, narrative drives price. And the market is changing. BTC doesn't need to do that well for alts to run. L1s are practically left on their own. People are focusing on what makes sense, and what accrues value. 

Nature is healing. 

Next post will be on tokens to focus on for the subscribers - ciao.

38 GW by 2032! I think the most important ingredient in recursive self improvement for AI is compute.

RSI is basically thousands of agents running small experiments in parallel, each using a small GPU cluster, say 4 nodes. Testing a training idea, changing an architecture, trying a different mix of data etc

Each agent writes detailed markdown explaining what it tried, what failed, what improved and what looks promising. Other agents read it and build on those findings. A shared research notebook that never stops growing.

You take the most promising ideas, check that the gains are real, and scale them up. The ones that still work at scale go into training a smarter model. That model runs better experiments, finds better improvements, and helps train the next one.

More compute lets you try more ideas at once AND find out faster whether they survive scaling. Both matter. A promising result on a small run is only the beginning.If this loop works reliably, compute becomes the fuel for an accelerating research process. Better models doing better research to build better models and then you have the beautiful RSI loop!
